analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income tax with a flat tax on wages and business income and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: S. 812 never got a cosponsor, a hearing, or a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from April 2005 until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: S. 812 would have scrapped the current income tax and replaced it with a single 20 percent tax on wages, salaries, and business income. Investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest would have gone untaxed, and the estate and gift taxes would have been repealed entirely. It would also have ended the public financing program for presidential campaigns and the funding mechanism for retired coal miners' health benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment income and large estates would gain the most: the bill taxed only wages and business profits, leaving interest, dividends, capital gains, and inheritances untaxed. Corporations and other businesses would gain from a flat 20 percent business tax in place of graduated rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors, large estates, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposed a single 20 percent rate on individual taxable earned income and on business taxable income, replacing the graduated income tax.
Earned income is defined as wages, salaries, and professional fees, so investment income such as interest, dividends, and capital gains would not be taxed at the individual level.
The bill repealed the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for decedents dying after December 31, 2005.

The bill allowed a standard deduction ($10,000 single, $20,000 joint, plus $5,000 per dependent), a capped charitable deduction of $2,500, and a home mortgage interest deduction, which would have simplified filing for many wage earners.

analysis.who_pays: Workers whose income comes only from wages would bear a flat 20 percent rate with few deductions, while the untaxed investment income flows to wealthier households; retired coal miners would lose the health benefits financing the bill repealed, and presidential campaigns would lose public funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners and retired coal miners

drawbacks.text: The bill taxed only earned income (wages, salaries, and professional fees), so households living on interest, dividends, and capital gains would pay no individual income tax while wage earners paid 20 percent on every dollar above the deductions.

A family of four would deduct $30,000 ($20,000 joint standard deduction plus $5,000 per dependent) and then pay 20 percent on the rest, with no child tax credit or earned income credit, which would raise the effective rate on many working families relative to current law.

The bill repealed the financing of presidential election campaigns and the coal industry retiree health benefits provisions, removing public funding from elections and the dedicated financing for retired miners' health care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real simplicity: a short tax code, a large standard deduction, and no more income tax on the middle of the return. But the core trade was to stop taxing income from wealth while keeping a flat 20 percent tax on income from work, which on its face shifts the tax burden toward wage earners and away from the households with the most investment income. The repeal of coal miner health benefits financing and public campaign financing were attached with no offsetting provisions. As written, the costs fell more heavily on ordinary workers than the benefits did.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the bill on April 15, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral for the remainder of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing graduated income tax, the estate tax, public financing of presidential campaigns, and the coal retiree health benefits financing all remained in place — the wage earners and retirees who would have borne the bill's costs were spared them, and no industry got the tax change it would have gained from.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners who kept the existing tax code

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act of 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 15, 2005 and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no party split ever formed.

industries.industry: High-income households living on investment income
industries.note: The bill taxed only wages, salaries, and business income, leaving interest, dividends, capital gains, and estates untaxed, so the households with the most wealth would have paid no individual income tax while wage earners paid 20 percent above the deductions.

The bill repealed the coal industry health benefits financing subtitle, ending the dedicated funding mechanism under which the industry supports retired miners' health care; the cost would have fallen on those retirees.

Businesses would have paid a flat 20 percent tax on active business income with full deduction of equipment and property costs, replacing graduated corporate rates; the offsetting revenue would have come from the flat tax on wages.
The bill barred businesses from deducting lobbying, political campaign, and grassroots lobbying expenditures, making influence spending more expensive for their clients.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Replacing the income tax with a short flat-tax code with a standard deduction, one charitable deduction, and a mortgage interest deduction would sharply reduce the complexity that tax filing businesses sell their services against.
